title: Easter, Lent and Shrovetide
when_text: Easter Sunday, the Sunday after the first full moon on or after the spring equinox (22 March to 25 April); Shrove Tuesday 47 days before, Maundy Thursday and Good Friday in the week before, Easter Monday the day after
intro: Easter is the Church's chief feast, and arguing over its date split the early English and Irish churches until the Synod of Whitby in 664. Around it grew the customs of the isles: pancakes and wild football matches on Shrove Tuesday before the Lenten fast, the monarch's Maundy alms, Easter sepulchres in parish churches, hot cross buns on Good Friday and egg rolling and bottle kicking on Easter Monday. Whether a goddess Eostre lent Easter its English name is still argued over.

facts.title: Two Easters at one court
facts.text: Irish-trained monks and those following Rome reckoned Easter differently, so that in Northumbria the queen could still be keeping the Lenten fast while the king celebrated Easter. At the Synod of Whitby in 664 King Oswiu ruled for the Roman reckoning.

sources.title: Synod of Whitby (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: King Oswiu ruled that his kingdom would calculate Easter and observe the monastic tonsure according to the customs of Rome rather than the customs practised by Irish monks at Iona

sources.title: Synod of Whitby (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: While one royal faction was celebrating Easter, the other would still be fasting during Lent.

facts.title: Was there a goddess Eostre?
facts.text: Bede, writing in the 720s, said the English name Easter came from Ēosturmōnaþ, the month (roughly April) named after a goddess Ēostre whose feasts the pagan English had kept. Whether Bede invented her has long been debated.

sources.title: Ēostre (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: He wrote that pagan Anglo-Saxons had held feasts in her honour during the month named after her: Ēosturmōnaþ (April), and that this became the English name for the Paschal season: Easter.

sources.title: Ēostre (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: It has been debated whether the goddess was an invention of Bede

facts.title: Shriven before Lent
facts.text: Shrove Tuesday takes its name from being shriven: people went to confession before Lent began. Around AD 1000 Ælfric of Eynsham told everyone to see their confessor in the week before Lent. Pancakes made a last rich meal before a fast that gave up meat, eggs and dairy foods.

sources.title: Shrove Tuesday (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The expression "Shrove Tuesday" comes from the word shrive, meaning absolution following confession.

sources.title: Shrove Tuesday (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: "In the week immediately before Lent everyone shall go to his confessor and confess his deeds

sources.title: Shrove Tuesday (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: believers have historically abstained from rich foods such as meat, eggs, lacticinia (dairy products), and alcohol

facts.title: The Olney pancake race
facts.text: Tradition in Olney says that on Shrove Tuesday 1445 a housewife heard the shriving bell and ran to church still holding her frying pan, tossing the pancake as she went. Women of the town race over 400 yards from the market place to the church of St Peter and St Paul each year, against a rival race in Liberal, Kansas.

where.name: Church of St Peter and St Paul, Olney

sources.title: Olney, Buckinghamshire (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Tradition records that on Shrove Tuesday 1445, the "Shriving Bell" signalled the start of the Shriving church service.

sources.title: Olney, Buckinghamshire (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The women of Olney recreate this event every Shrove Tuesday by running from the market place to the Church of St Peter & St Paul, a distance of over 400 yards.

sources.title: Olney, Buckinghamshire (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Olney now competes with the town of Liberal, Kansas, USA, for the fastest time in either town to win the "International Pancake Race".

facts.title: Ashbourne's two-day football match
facts.text: In Ashbourne, Derbyshire, the town plays a football game through the town on Shrove Tuesday and Ash Wednesday, from 2 pm to 10 pm, with goals three miles apart at two mills. Those born north of Henmore Brook play those born south. It goes back to at least about 1667 (a fire destroyed older records) and has been "Royal" since the Prince of Wales started it in 1928, when he got a bloody nose.

sources.title: Royal Shrovetide Football (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: has been played from at least c.1667 although the exact origins of the game are unknown due to a fire at the Royal Shrovetide Committee office in the 1890s which destroyed the earliest records

sources.title: Royal Shrovetide Football (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: There are two goal posts 3 miles (4.8 km) apart, one at Sturston Mill (where the Up'Ards attempt to score), the other at Clifton Mill (where the Down'Ards score).

sources.title: Royal Shrovetide Football (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The Up'Ards are traditionally those town members born north of Henmore Brook

sources.title: Royal Shrovetide Football (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The game has been known as "Royal" since 1928, when the then-Prince of Wales (later King Edward VIII) turned up the ball.

sources.title: Royal Shrovetide Football (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: starting each day at 2:00 pm and lasting until 10:00 pm

facts.title: Atherstone's match for a bag of gold
facts.text: Atherstone in Warwickshire plays a two-hour scramble for a giant ball along its main street every Shrove Tuesday, said to honour a match of 1199 between Warwickshire and Leicestershire for a bag of gold put up by King John. It is one of three Shrovetide street games left in England, with Ashbourne and Scoring the Hales at Alnwick; one of its few rules is that no one may be killed.

sources.title: Atherstone Ball Game (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The original medieval football game honoured by the annual event was held in Atherstone in 1199, during which teams from Warwickshire and Leicestershire competed to win a bag of gold offered as a prize by King John.

sources.title: Atherstone Ball Game (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: the other two being the Royal Shrovetide Football match in Ashbourne, Derbyshire, and Scoring the Hales in Alnwick, Northumberland

sources.title: Atherstone Ball Game (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The game itself has few rules, two being that play is restricted to Long Street and participants are not allowed to kill anyone.

facts.title: King John's Maundy
facts.text: The first English king recorded giving Maundy alms was John, at Knaresborough on 15 April 1210; in 1213 at Rochester he gave thirteen poor men thirteen pence each. Today the monarch hands out specially struck silver Maundy money, as many pence as the sovereign's years of age.

sources.title: Royal Maundy (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The first English monarch to be recorded as distributing alms at a Maundy service was John, who on 15 April 1210 donated garments, forks, food, and other gifts to the poor of Knaresborough, Yorkshire.

sources.title: Royal Maundy (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: when in 1213 he gave 13 pence to each of 13 poor men at a ceremony in Rochester

sources.title: Royal Maundy (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: a white one containing coins to the value of the same number of pence as the years of the monarch's age

facts.title: The last royal foot-washing
facts.text: Medieval monarchs washed the feet of beggars on Maundy Thursday, as Jesus washed his disciples' feet. James II is usually said to have been the last to do it himself, in 1685, though William III is recorded doing so in 1698.

sources.title: Royal Maundy (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: In the Middle Ages, English monarchs washed the feet of beggars in imitation of Jesus, and presented gifts and money to the poor.

sources.title: Royal Maundy (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Although there is a record of William III doing so in 1698, most sources state that James was the last to wash the feet of the poor himself, in 1685.

facts.title: Christ's tomb in the parish church
facts.text: Medieval churches kept an Easter sepulchre, usually an arched recess in the north wall of the chancel, where the crucifix and the consecrated host were laid from Good Friday to Easter Day. Most were wooden and have gone, but carved stone ones survive, as at Hawton in Nottinghamshire and Heckington in Lincolnshire.

sources.title: Easter Sepulchre (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The Easter Sepulchre is an arched recess generally in the north wall of the chancel, in which from Good Friday to Easter day were deposited the crucifix and sacred elements in commemoration of Christ's entombment and resurrection.

sources.title: Easter Sepulchre (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: It was generally only a wooden structure, which was placed in a recess or on a tomb.

sources.title: All Saints' Church, Hawton (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: On the north side of the chancel is a medieval Easter Sepulchre.

facts.title: Hot cross buns
facts.text: In 1592 London's Clerk of Markets banned the sale of spiced buns except at burials, on Good Friday and at Christmas. The first definite mention of hot cross buns by name is a street cry printed in Poor Robin's Almanac for 1733.

sources.title: Hot cross bun (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: In 1592, during the reign of Elizabeth I of England, the London Clerk of Markets issued a decree forbidding the sale of spiced buns and other spiced breads except at burials, on Good Friday, or at Christmas.

sources.title: Hot cross bun (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: which appeared in Poor Robin's Almanac for 1733

facts.title: Pace eggs rolled downhill
facts.text: Rolling decorated eggs down grassy slopes, part of "pace-egging", has gone on for centuries in the north of England and in Scotland, at places such as Avenham Park in Preston, Penshaw Hill and Arthur's Seat in Edinburgh. Pace-eggers in fancy dress went round singing and performing mumming plays.

sources.title: Egg rolling (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: In the United Kingdom the tradition of rolling decorated eggs down grassy hills goes back hundreds of years and is known as "pace-egging".

sources.title: Egg rolling (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Other traditional egg rolling sites are the castle moat at Penrith, Bunkers Hill in Derby, Arthur's Seat in Edinburgh, Hill 60 on the Beverley Westwood and on Penshaw Hill in Tyne and Wear at Penshaw Monument.

sources.title: Egg rolling (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: In Scotland, pace-eggin is traditional from Shetland to The Borders

facts.title: Hare pie and bottle kicking
facts.text: Every Easter Monday Hallaton in Leicestershire fights neighbouring Medbourne for small wooden barrels ("bottles"). Local lore says two women saved from a bull by a hare gave land to the church on condition the vicar provided a hare pie, bread and ale each Easter Monday; when a rector tried to stop it in 1790, "No pie, no parson" appeared on his wall.

where.name: Church of St Michael and All Angels, Hallaton

sources.title: Bottle-kicking (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: To show their gratitude to God for sending the hare, they made a gift of land to the church, on the understanding that every Easter Monday, the vicar would provide a hare pie, twelve penny loaves, and two barrels of ale for the poor of the village.

sources.title: Bottle-kicking (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: However, he relented the next day, after the words "No pie, no parson" appeared scrawled on the wall of the vicarage overnight.

sources.title: Bottle-kicking (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: two teams attempt to move a wooden barrel (known as a "bottle") across the opposing team's stream

facts.title: The Tichborne Dole and its curse
facts.text: At Tichborne in Hampshire flour is given to the villagers at Lady Day (the Annunciation, 25 March), a dole said to have been begun about 1150 by Lady Mabella Tichborne, who crawled round a 23-acre field with a burning torch to win the land for it. She cursed the family if it stopped: it was halted in 1796, the baronet of seven sons then had seven daughters, and the dole was restored.

sources.title: Tichborne Dole (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: held in the village of Tichborne, Hampshire, during the Feast of the Annunciation

sources.title: Lady Day (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Lady Day is the common name in some English-speaking countries of the Feast of the Annunciation, celebrated on 25 March

sources.title: Tichborne Dole (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: is said to have successfully crawled around a 23-acre (93,000 m2) field before the torch went out

sources.title: Tichborne Dole (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: was the eldest of seven sons. He had seven daughters but no sons.

facts.title: Equinox sunrise in Cairn T
facts.text: Easter is reckoned from the spring equinox. At Loughcrew in County Meath the passage of Cairn T, a Neolithic tomb, faces the rising sun at the spring and autumn equinoxes, when light reaches the carved backstone of the chamber; people gather there to watch it.

sources.title: Easter (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: established common Paschal observance by all Christians on the first Sunday after the first full moon on or after the vernal equinox

sources.title: Loughcrew (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Cairn T in Carnbane East is directed to receive the beams of the rising sun on the spring and autumnal equinox - the light shining down the passage and illuminating the art on the backstone.

sources.title: Loughcrew Cairns (Heritage Ireland)
sources.author: OPW
sources.quote: The cairn is aligned to sunrise at the spring and autumn equinoxes and at these times people gather there to greet the first rays of the sun.

places.why: Abbess Hild's monastery, where the Synod of 664 settled how Northumbria reckoned Easter; the later Benedictine church ruins are in the care of English Heritage.

sources.title: Whitby Abbey (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: In 664, the Synod of Whitby took place at the monastery to resolve the question of whether the Northumbrian church would adopt and follow the Easter dating of Iona

sources.title: Whitby Abbey (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: the substantial ruins of the church have been declared a Grade I Listed building and are in the care of English Heritage

sources.title: Olney, Buckinghamshire (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The women of Olney recreate this event every Shrove Tuesday by running from the market place to the Church of St Peter & St Paul

sources.title: Olney, Buckinghamshire (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors

places.name: Ashbourne
places.why: Derbyshire market town of Royal Shrovetide Football: the ball is turned up from a plinth in the town centre, and goal scorers are carried into the courtyard of the Green Man Royal Hotel.

sources.title: Royal Shrovetide Football (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: the scorer is carried on the shoulders of his colleagues into the courtyard of the Green Man Royal Hotel

places.name: Atherstone
places.why: Warwickshire town whose Long Street is the pitch of the Shrove Tuesday ball game.

sources.title: Atherstone Ball Game (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The two-hour game is played in the town's main street, Long Street

places.name: All Saints' Church, Hawton
places.why: Its chancel, which Pevsner thought one of the most exciting pieces of architecture in the country, has a famous medieval Easter sepulchre on the north side.

sources.title: All Saints' Church, Hawton (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Most famous is the Easter Sepulchre, which would have been used to reserve the consecrated bread and wine between Maundy Thursday and Easter Day

sources.title: All Saints' Church, Hawton (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: one of the most exciting pieces of architecture in the country.

places.name: Church of St Andrew, Heckington
places.why: Fourteenth-century Lincolnshire church whose richly carved Easter sepulchre is one of the most celebrated in England.

sources.title: Church of St Andrew, Heckington (British Listed Buildings, from the Historic England list entry 1360590)
sources.author: Historic England
sources.quote: The Easter sepulchre, one of the most celebrated English examples, consists of a small triangular central niche in a tripartite stone framework.

places.name: Westminster Abbey
places.why: Where the Royal Maundy service was held in most years of the early and mid 20th century; it now moves to a different church, usually a cathedral, each year.

sources.title: Royal Maundy (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Traditionally, the service was held in or near London, in most years in the early-to-mid-20th century at Westminster Abbey; the service is now held in a different church (usually a cathedral) every year.

places.name: Avenham Park
places.why: Preston park where Easter egg rolling has gone on for hundreds of years, now with chocolate eggs.

sources.title: Egg rolling (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Egg rolling has been a tradition at Avenham Park for hundreds of years, but in recent years chocolate eggs have been used.

places.name: Penshaw Monument
places.why: Hilltop temple on Penshaw Hill in Tyne and Wear, one of the traditional places for rolling Easter eggs.

sources.title: Egg rolling (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: on Penshaw Hill in Tyne and Wear at Penshaw Monument

places.name: Church of St Michael and All Angels, Hallaton
places.why: Mainly 13th-century church with a fine broach spire; the land given to it is the source, in local lore, of the Easter Monday hare pie scramble and bottle kicking.

sources.title: Hallaton (Wikipedia)
